steps.step: A filter's contents depend only on which bit positions have been set to 1. Adding an item sets that item's k positions to 1 and changes nothing else.
steps.part: The parts (Add(x) and Query(x) operations; Hash function: the same item always gives the same number)
steps.idea: Add computes k positions from the item alone and sets them to 1. Because the hashes are deterministic, an item lands on the same positions in any filter that has the same m and the same hash functions.

steps.step: A bit is 1 in a filter exactly when at least one added item maps to it. Adding the same item twice, or adding items in a different order, gives the same array.
steps.part: Why it never misses an item it saw (Add only changes bits from 0 to 1; nothing clears a bit)
steps.idea: Bits only go from 0 to 1 and never back. So the final array is the union of every added item's positions, whatever the order and however many repeats.

steps.step: The filter you would build from A ∪ B has a 1 at bit i exactly when some item in A or some item in B maps to i. That is the same as: bit i is 1 in filter A, or bit i is 1 in filter B.
steps.idea: Each item in A ∪ B lies in A or in B, and it sets the same positions in either filter. So the union filter's set bits are exactly the bits set in A's filter together with those set in B's filter.

steps.step: Taking the bitwise OR of the two arrays therefore gives the A ∪ B filter, with no access to the items. The result is exact: it is the same bit array you would get by adding every item of A ∪ B to an empty filter.
steps.idea: OR is 1 exactly when either input bit is 1, which is the condition from step 3.

steps.step: The merged filter works like a filter holding all of A ∪ B, so its error rate follows from that larger number of items.
steps.part: How often it is wrong; What happens when the filter fills up
steps.idea: The false-positive rate p ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k uses the total number of items in the filter, here |A ∪ B|. The merge itself adds no error, but a fuller array means more false positives.

steps.step: Bitwise AND gives 1 only where both filters have a 1. Every item in A ∩ B sets its k bits in both filters, so all of its bits survive the AND. A query for such an item still says 'probably seen': there are no false negatives for the intersection.
steps.part: Steps 1–2; Why it never misses an item it saw
steps.idea: An item in both sets maps to the same positions in both arrays, and those bits are 1 in each, so they are 1 after the AND.

steps.step: AND is not exact for A ∩ B. A bit can be 1 in both filters because one item of A and a different item of B happen to share it, even when no common item maps there. So the AND result can have more 1s than the filter you would build from A ∩ B directly.
steps.part: A worked example ("cat" and "dog" share bit 6; the filter has no record of which item set a bit)
steps.idea: Different items can share bits, and the filter cannot tell who set a bit. So 'set in both filters' does not mean 'set by an item that is in both sets'.

steps.step: The AND result therefore contains every bit of the true A ∩ B filter, plus possibly some extra bits. It still gives no false negatives, but its false-positive rate can be higher than that of a filter built directly from A ∩ B.
steps.part: Steps 6–7; How often it is wrong
steps.idea: Extra 1s make it more likely that all k bits of an absent item are 1, which is exactly the false-positive condition.

result: Take the bitwise OR of the two bit arrays. Because every item sets the same positions in both filters and bits only ever go from 0 to 1, the OR is exactly the filter you would get by adding every item of A ∪ B, so the union is exact. Its error rate is the normal one for |A ∪ B| items in m bits. The bitwise AND gives a filter that says 'probably seen' for every item in A ∩ B, so it has no false negatives, but it is not exact. Bits set by different items in A and in B can collide and survive the AND, so it may have extra 1s compared with the true A ∩ B filter, and therefore more false positives. It is a safe approximation, not the true intersection filter.
